papers.title: Quantification of the healthy worker effect: a nationwide cohort study among electricians in Denmark.
papers.one_line: A Danish register cohort of all men aged 26-56 in 1984-1992 compared four bias-control strategies for the healthy worker effect and found that the marginal structural model failed to move the mortality rate ratio toward the null while a three-year lag brought it from 0.60 to 0.92.
papers.what_was_done: All Danish male citizens aged 26-56 in 1984-1992 were followed three years through national registers, with electricians used as an occupational group free of harmful exposures so that any exposure-outcome association measures bias rather than effect. Electricians had a mortality rate ratio of 0.60 (95% CI 0.52 to 0.69) against the general population, while electricians who left employment had a rate ratio of 1.90 (1.50 to 2.40), rising to 15.7 for those on long-term sick leave. Restricting to persons employed in year 2 moved the estimate for electricians employed only in year 0 further from the null, to 2.17 (1.62 to 2.91), consistent with collider stratification on employment status. A marginal structural model was fitted as a stabilized inverse-probability-weighted Poisson regression with mean, minimum and maximum weights of 1.00, 0.78 and 76.43; it did not attenuate the bias in any of the three reference-group comparisons. Comparison against two occupational reference groups, construction industry and carpenters or brick layers, removed most of the gap, and a lag of three or more years gave 0.92 (0.82 to 1.04). No sensitivity analysis quantified how much of the residual gap remained after each strategy, and the weight distribution was reported without identifying which employment histories carried the extreme weights.

future_research.gap: Whether a lag length that works for all-cause mortality transfers to other outcomes is unresolved, and the lag was chosen by inspecting how far each candidate moved the estimate.
future_research.quote: It should be emphasized that our suggested lag time of three or more years may only be relevant for our specific outcome

future_research.gap: Reference-group selection as a bias-control strategy depends on register coverage that most settings lack.
future_research.quote: our result of minimizing of HWE bias by lag time analyses may be applicable

problems.evidence: Four analytic strategies applied to the same register data give mortality rate ratios of 0.60, 2.17, 0.92 and a weighted estimate that moved in the wrong direction, with no criterion offered to prefer one. The weighted Poisson model is the estimator with the strongest theoretical warrant for time-varying confounding and it is the one that failed. Nothing in the reporting requires an emulation to show that its estimator choice was not the driver of its answer.
problems.quote: we implemented the marginal structural model, which rather surprisingly did not minimize HWE bias

problems.evidence: Positivity is reported as three numbers describing the weight distribution, a mean of 1.00 against a maximum of 76.43, meaning at least one person carried roughly 76 times the influence of an average person. The report never names which combinations of social event, employment status and comorbidity index produced that weight, so a reader cannot tell which worker histories the pseudo-population extrapolated into.
problems.quote: In Model 4, MSM was implemented with estimated weights of 1.00, 0.78 and 76.43 as the mean, minimum and maximum weights.

problems.evidence: The lag length was selected by scanning candidate lags until the electrician rate ratio reached 0.92 (0.82 to 1.04), an interval containing the null. That is selection of a timing parameter on the basis of the outcome estimate it produces, and the acknowledgment that the chosen lag is specific to all-cause mortality confirms that no outcome-blind rule generated it.
problems.quote: It should be emphasized that our suggested lag time of three or more years may only be relevant for our specific outcome

problems.evidence: Restricting the cohort to persons actively employed is an eligibility rule built from an administrative record of continued participation, and it moved the estimate for short-term electricians from the multivariable value to 2.17 (1.62 to 2.91), further from the null rather than closer. Employment status sits downstream of occupation and upstream of mortality, so the restriction opens a path through unmeasured health.
problems.quote: restriction could introduce collider bias between Elec0 and UH1, resulting in a negative association between Elec0 and UH1

problems.evidence: The design supplies a working negative-control procedure: an occupation with no known harmful exposure is used so that any nonzero rate ratio is bias, and three reference groups calibrate its magnitude, yielding 0.60 against the general population versus 1.01 (0.87 to 1.19) against the construction industry. That converts residual confounding into a measured quantity. It does not close the entry: the negative control is not paired with a proxy or validation dataset, no threshold declares the residual bias acceptable, and nothing in the reporting standard requires such a control.
problems.quote: We evaluated HWE bias among electricians because they were unexposed to detrimental occupational exposures.

problems.evidence: When the weighted model failed, the explanation offered was that the assumed causal diagram might be wrong, an assumption for which the data carry no diagnostic. The diagram sits alongside no-unmeasured-confounding and correct weight specification, and the report distinguishes none of them by whether evidence could bear on it.
problems.quote: One reason could be that employment status in year 1 (Emp1) was only partly associated with UH1 and that the setup in Figure 1 therefore was incorrect.

papers.title: Testing and estimating model-adjusted effect-measure modification using marginal structural models and complex survey data.
papers.one_line: Standardized risk differences for disability and cost barriers to care in 31,590 Florida survey respondents were estimated two ways, and the youngest age group came out at 0.107 under exposure modeling versus 0.158 under outcome modeling, with neither approach preferable on the data.
papers.what_was_done: Two routes to model-based standardization on complex survey data are set out and compared on the 2007 Florida Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System, restricted to 31,590 complete records after excluding anyone missing race, income, education or gender. The marginal structural model route weights each record by the product of the survey weight, which maps the sample to the unstandardized population, and an inverse-probability-of-exposure weight estimated using those same survey weights, which standardizes for race, income, education and gender. The alternative averages risks from a standard survey logistic regression. Both find heterogeneity of the disability-associated risk difference across age with P below 0.001, but they disagree on magnitude: for ages 18 to 29 the weighted route gives 0.107 and the risk-averaging route gives 0.158 (95% CI 0.023 to 0.293); for ages 65 and over they give 0.021 and 0.032. Variance is obtained by Taylor linearization, which is correct only when the weights are known, so intervals from the weighted route are conservative when the weights are estimated. A simulation drew 500 complex survey samples averaging 2,267 records from an initial 3,500. Missingness was handled by deletion rather than by a third weight term.

future_research.gap: A doubly robust estimator for complex survey data does not exist yet.
future_research.quote: We are currently working on developing a doubly robust procedure for complex survey data.

problems.evidence: A concrete procedure is supplied for stacking a sampling assumption on a confounding assumption: the analysis weight is the product of the survey weight and an inverse-probability-of-exposure weight, and the second must itself be estimated using the first, with code given. That makes the two-stage structure explicit rather than implicit. It does not close the entry: the uncertainty from the two layers is not separated, the interval is only known to be conservative rather than correct, and no sensitivity analysis probes the sampling model the way the confounding model is probed.
problems.quote: The second term is an inverse-probability-of-exposure weight that standardizes the population in order to adjust for confounding; it must be estimated using the survey weights.

problems.evidence: On 31,590 records the two estimators disagree by 0.05 on the absolute risk scale in the youngest age group, 0.107 against 0.158, which is a third of the estimate itself, and the response is to wonder what a third estimator would give. Each route is valid only if its own model is correct, and no data-driven check adjudicates between them.
problems.quote: The difference in estimates for the youngest age group (18–25 years) from the 2 approaches leads us naturally to wonder what results a doubly robust procedure (17) would give.

problems.evidence: The Taylor-linearization variance is correct only for known weights; because the exposure weights were fitted, the reported intervals are conservative by an unquantified amount. The exact alternative named is a nonparametric bootstrap that refits the weights in every replicate, which multiplies the cost of the weight estimation by the number of replicates and is offered without a scalable default.
problems.quote: The first method leads to confidence intervals and hypothesis tests that are asymptotically conservative because of the estimated weights; a nonparametric bootstrap approach would produce asymptotically exact results.

problems.evidence: Positivity enters only as an algebraic remark that the exposure probability must be bounded away from zero because the weight divides by it. No diagnostic identifies which combinations of race, income, education, gender and age category approach that boundary, even though the age-stratified risk differences are the reported quantity and the 18 to 29 stratum is the one where the two methods diverge most.
problems.quote: the exposure modeling approach can only be used when P(XjM,Z) is

problems.evidence: Records with any missing key variable were deleted outright, and the remedy contemplated is a third inverse-probability-of-complete-observation factor multiplied into the existing weight. Observation is thereby treated as a nuisance to be reweighted away rather than as a process that might be caused by disability status or by cost barriers, which are precisely the exposure and the outcome.
problems.quote: the combined weights could accommodate a third term representing the inverse probability of a complete observation

papers.title: Dynamic regime marginal structural mean models for estimation of optimal dynamic treatment regimes, Part II: proofs of results.
papers.one_line: The proof companion for dynamic-regime marginal structural mean models, whose positivity worked example shows that support is required only for histories consistent with the regime and that a confidence set for the optimal regime index reduces to a half-space feasibility problem rather than a standard variance calculation.
papers.what_was_done: Proofs are supplied for the identification and estimation claims of the companion paper on marginal structural mean models indexed by dynamic regimes, together with a procedure for a confidence set for the optimal regime index when the index set is finite, and a worked example of the positivity assumption. In the example the horizon is two decision points with binary covariate and binary treatment and no deaths, so the regime assigns treatment as one minus the first covariate and then as a product rule at the second point. Positivity then reduces to four conditional probabilities being nonzero at the first point and four more at the second, each naming a specific covariate and treatment history. The example establishes that support is required only among people whose observed history is compatible with the regime, and that people who already deviated carry no information about the regime-specific outcome distribution. The confidence set for the optimal index is built by testing whether the intersection of a set of half-spaces with a ball centered at the origin is nonempty, one test per candidate index. No data, no sample size and no simulation appear; the paper is entirely analytic.

problems.evidence: The positivity requirement is translated from a statement about weights into an explicit list of histories that must be populated: for the two-point binary example it names the four covariate-treatment strata that must contain subjects following the regime, and it establishes that no support is needed among people who already deviated. That is exactly the naming of unsupported histories the entry asks for. It does not close the entry: the enumeration is done by hand for a toy example with two binary times, there is no finite-sample near-violation measure, and nothing scales the enumeration to the covariate histories of a real emulation.
problems.quote: the requirement that in the actual world there be subjects with L0 = 0 that take treatment A0 = 1 and subjects with L0 = 1 that take treatment A0 = 0

problems.evidence: The example makes explicit that when a regime-compatible stratum is empty, no estimation strategy recovers the regime-specific outcome distribution in that stratum; the requirement is on the observed data, not on the model. This is the boundary that flexible fitting cannot cross, and the argument holds for the doubly robust estimators the companion paper develops as much as for the weighted ones.
problems.quote: we must observe people in the study that obeyed the treatment at every level of

problems.evidence: Inference for the index of the optimal regime is not a variance estimate at all: it requires a separate construction that tests, for each of the candidate indices, whether the intersection of the half-spaces induced by the other candidates with a confidence ball is nonempty. The cost grows with the number of candidate regimes and with the dimension of the model parameter, and no scalable default is offered for the case where the index set is not finite.
problems.quote: a proposal for the computation of a confidence set for the optimal index when this lies in a finite set

problems.evidence: Identification is worked out on a fixed discrete grid of decision points with the covariate process observed at every one of them, and the illustrative case sets survival to one with probability one so that the observation process is deterministic. Nothing in the development covers decision times generated by the treatment process itself or covariates observed only when a visit happens.
problems.quote: so that no subject dies in neither the actual world nor in the hypothetical world in which g is enforced in the population

papers.title: Attributable fractions for sufficient cause interactions.
papers.one_line: A theory paper showing that etiologic fractions for sufficient cause interactions are only bounded below, not point identified, and that under time-dependent confounding the counterfactual expectations the bounds require are not identified at all.
papers.what_was_done: The excess fraction, the share of disease removable by eliminating a mechanism, is separated from the etiologic fraction, the share caused by it, and both are worked out for the sufficient cause containing two or more binary exposures. Under monotonicity an exact formula for the excess fraction is given; without monotonicity, and for etiologic fractions in every case, only lower bounds are available, computed as a sum over covariate strata of a maximum against zero. A weighting procedure is proposed that estimates these bounds from a marginal structural model rather than an outcome regression, on the argument that a regression forces a functional relation between the confounders and the unobserved background causes. A published proposal by Hoffmann and colleagues is shown to require monotonicity that the proposal did not state. In the presence of a time-varying covariate caused by the first exposure and causing both the second exposure and the outcome, sequential ignorability identifies expectations conditional on covariates but not the expectations conditional on both exposures being present, which are exactly the quantities the bounds use; one additional homogeneity restriction restores identification. Whether the bounds are sharp is left unresolved, and no data application, sample size or interval estimate appears.

future_research.gap: Whether sharper lower bounds on etiologic fractions exist is unresolved.
future_research.quote: Whether bounds sharper than this can be obtained is an open question.

problems.evidence: A published attributable-fraction procedure is shown to have depended on monotonicity that its own report never listed, and monotonicity is untestable from the data that the procedure consumes. The bounds derived here change form depending on whether monotonicity holds, so the assumption is load-bearing for the number reported. Nothing in the reporting format separates an assumption a reader could probe from one that only substantive argument can support.
problems.quote: We argue that the approach proposed by Hoffmann et al. implicitly requires monotonicity assumptions that are not acknowledged in the paper.

problems.evidence: Moving from outcome regression to a weighted marginal structural model relaxes modeling restrictions but does not restore identification: under the time-varying confounder structure examined, the conditional counterfactual expectations that the etiologic-fraction bound requires remain unidentified for the untreated level of the first exposure, a conjecture of Robins later confirmed by graphical identification rules. The remedy that works is an extra homogeneity restriction on the covariate-conditional contrast, not a more flexible estimator.
problems.quote: would not be identi ed if
problems.locator: Time-Dependent Confounding in Inference for Etiologic Fractions

problems.evidence: Two estimators of the same attributable fraction are compared on the plausibility of the modeling assumptions each imposes, weighting against outcome regression, with the choice argued rather than measured. No diagnostic distinguishes a setting where the restriction on confounders and background causes bites from one where it does not, so the preference cannot be checked against data.
problems.quote: this approach based on marginal structural models is preferable to a regression approach because it does not impose restrictions on the relationship between the confounding variables and the potentially unknown background

problems.evidence: The scientific target is the share of disease due to a specific mechanism, but what is reportable is a lower bound on that share, and the gap between the two is never quantified. A reader receives one number with no decomposition into how much is genuine mechanism, how much is bound slack from unidentified counterfactuals, and how much is sampling error.
problems.quote: When etiologic fractions are of interest or when monotonicity assumptions do not hold for excess fractions then only lower bounds can be given.

papers.title: Time scale and adjusted survival curves for marginal structural cox models.
papers.one_line: Switching the time scale of a marginal structural Cox model from time on study to time on treatment moved the hazard ratio for antiretroviral therapy from 0.52 to 0.44 and turned a nonsignificant proportional-hazards interaction, P equal to 0.268, into a significant one, P equal to 0.017, on the same 1,498 people.
papers.what_was_done: The total effect of highly active antiretroviral therapy on AIDS or death was estimated in 1,498 HIV-positive United States men and women contributing 6,556 person-years between 1995 and 2002, with 323 incident AIDS cases and 59 deaths, and 77 percent of the remaining 1,116 still under observation at the end. Inverse probability of treatment and censoring weights accounted for age, race, sex, baseline and current CD4 count, baseline and current HIV RNA, follow-up time, calendar time, Pneumocystis prophylaxis and non-HAART antiretroviral therapy. On time on study the weighted hazard ratio was 0.52 (95% CI 0.35 to 0.76); on time on treatment it was 0.44 (0.32 to 0.60), a 1.18-fold stronger estimate with a 1.16-fold tighter interval. Splitting at the median event time, 87 weeks on study and 58 weeks on treatment, the time-on-study contrast moved from 0.68 to 0.46 with interaction P equal to 0.268 while the time-on-treatment contrast moved from 0.61 to 0.32 with interaction P equal to 0.017. Weighted Kaplan-Meier curves were produced by dropping baseline covariates from the weight numerator. Treatment was carried forward after initiation, misclassifying 6 percent of person-time.

future_research.gap: Defining time on treatment for people who start and stop is unresolved and was avoided by an assumption rather than solved.
future_research.quote: First, defining time on treatment is complicated if participants move on and off treatment during follow-up.

problems.evidence: One structural choice about the time axis, made after the data were in hand, changed the hazard ratio from 0.52 to 0.44 and flipped the verdict on proportional hazards from P equal to 0.268 to P equal to 0.017. Both analyses use the same 1,498 people, the same 382 events and the same weights, so the difference is entirely the metric on which risk sets are formed, and no outcome-blind rule chose it.
problems.quote: In the example presented, using time on treatment as the time scale yielded a 1.18-fold stronger estimate of the hazard ratio (0.44 compared with 0.52) and a 1.16-fold tighter confidence interval than using time on study as the time scale.

problems.evidence: The two time scales define different estimands, not two estimates of one: time on study averages the hazard ratio across a sequence of trials randomized at every timepoint, while time on treatment averages over time since initiation. Both are reported as the hazard ratio for always versus never using therapy, and the inclusion of baseline covariates in the final structural model further renders the reported quantity conditional rather than marginal.
problems.quote: using time on study as the time scale, the marginal structural model recovers the average hazard ratio across a series of randomized trials, with randomization at each sequential timepoint

problems.evidence: The time scale is declared more appropriate because 0.44 sits nearer a published trial hazard ratio of 0.50 (0.33 to 0.76) than 0.52 does, with the residual gap explained away by a different comparator and by trial noncompliance. That is a proximity judgment on a point estimate, not a calibrated comparison: no interval overlap statistic, no accounting for the differing estimands and no prespecified equivalence margin is offered.
problems.quote: Time-on-treatment results are closer to what we would expect from a randomized trial of HAART versus non-HAART.

problems.evidence: Therapy is treated as absorbing once initiated, so all regimen versions after initiation collapse into one, and the price is stated as 6 percent of person-time misclassified. No procedure defines which interruptions and restarts belong in the same class as continuous therapy; the equivalence was imposed to make time on treatment definable at all.
problems.quote: This intent-to-treat assumption renders the complication of participants moving on and off treatment moot, at the cost of misclassifying 6% of person-time.

problems.evidence: Reading the time-on-study analysis as an average across trials randomized at each sequential timepoint puts calendar time at the center, and calendar time is a strong confounder here because therapy availability changed sharply between 1995 and 2002. The two time scales require subtly different calendar-time specifications in the structural model, and the report gives no rule for getting that right.
problems.quote: there are subtly different specifications for the effect of calendar time in the structural models under the 2 time scales; care must be taken when (as in this case) calendar time is a strong confounder

papers.title: Marginal structural models for sufficient cause interactions.
papers.one_line: Weighting rather than outcome regression is used to test for mechanistic interaction between arsenic and smoking on skin lesions, giving an interaction coefficient of 3.64 per 100 with a confidence interval of 0.13 to 7.14 that depends entirely on an untestable monotonicity assumption.
papers.what_was_done: A marginal structural model with weights formed as the product of two separate inverse-probability-of-exposure terms is proposed as an alternative to outcome regression for testing whether a causal mechanism requires two exposures jointly. The argument is that an outcome regression constrains the relation between the confounders and the unobserved background causes of the sufficient cause framework, whereas weighting constrains the relation between the exposures and the confounders instead. The illustration dichotomizes well arsenic at a high level and smoking, in a Bangladeshi population with skin lesions as outcome, adjusting for sex, age, education, body mass index, land and television ownership, fertilizer use and pesticide use. Weights were truncated at the first and ninety-ninth percentiles. Per 100, the fitted coefficients were 4.72 (95% CI 3.40 to 6.04) for the intercept, 3.03 (0.66 to 5.40) and 1.72 (-0.13 to 3.57) for the two main effects, and 3.64 (0.13 to 7.14) for the interaction, read as a lower bound of 3.64 percent on the prevalence of individuals whose lesion requires both exposures. Because the interaction coefficient is smaller than the intercept, the conclusion holds only under monotonicity. The number of participants, the arsenic cutpoint value and the truncated weight distribution are not reported.

future_research.gap: Binary coding of the two exposures is a placeholder; the appropriate cutpoints and ordinal treatment of arsenic are unresolved.
future_research.quote: In future work, it may be of interest to treat arsenic and smoking as ordinal rather than binary variables

future_research.gap: Which exposure measure and which cutpoint the analysis should use is unsettled.
future_research.quote: full analysis of a variety of measures for arsenic, more relevant exposure cutpoints, and interactions between a variety of environmental exposures is a topic of current research

problems.evidence: Arsenic exposure is collapsed to a single high-versus-low indicator at an unstated cutpoint, and the analysis itself records that the cutpoint is provisional and that ordinal handling belongs to future work. The interaction estimate of 3.64 per 100 is defined relative to that dichotomy, so a different equivalence class of arsenic exposure defines a different mechanism and a different bound. No procedure selects the cutpoint on clinical grounds.
problems.quote: full analysis of a variety of measures for arsenic, more relevant exposure cutpoints, and interactions between a variety of environmental exposures is a topic of current research

problems.evidence: Positivity is handled by truncating the product weight at the first and ninety-ninth percentiles, which is a rule about the weight distribution and not about people. Two percent of the sample therefore has its influence reset by fiat, and the report does not say which combinations of sex, age, socioeconomic markers and pesticide use those observations had, so a reader cannot tell whether the arsenic-and-smoking cell was supported in the covariate regions that drive the 3.64 estimate.
problems.quote: Following suggestions about truncation from Cole and Hernán (18), weights are truncated at the 1st and 99th percentiles.

problems.evidence: The entire conclusion rests on monotonicity, and the analysis states that without it no conclusion follows because the interaction coefficient of 3.64 falls below the intercept of 4.72. Monotonicity is defended by biological argument alone and no data feature could contradict it, yet it is presented in the same register as no unmeasured confounding, which at least admits negative-control probes.
problems.quote: it is not possible to draw conclusions about sufficient cause interactions without the monotonicity assumption

problems.evidence: Four separate objections are raised against the outcome-regression route to the same target, covering main-effect misspecification, out-of-range fitted values, effect heterogeneity in the confounders and restrictions on background causes. The weighted alternative trades those for correct specification of two exposure models, and no diagnostic is given that would tell an analyst which trade is better in a given dataset.
problems.quote: The regression approach to testing for sufficient cause interactions can be problematic for several reasons.

problems.evidence: The headline quantity is a lower bound of 3.64 percent whose interval runs from 0.13 to 7.14, a width of 7 percentage points on a bound that has to exceed zero to mean anything. That width comes from estimating a four-parameter model on the product of two truncated weight series, so the effective information behind the interaction cell is far smaller than the nominal sample.
problems.quote: An estimate of the lower bound on the prevalence of such sufficient cause interactions is 3.64%, but the confidence interval is quite wide

papers.title: Targeted maximum likelihood based causal inference: Part I.
papers.one_line: The targeted maximum likelihood framework for multiple time point interventions, which states plainly that cross-validated super learning of the nuisance factors is biased for a smooth causal parameter because cross-validation optimizes a global loss whose scale exceeds that of the target.
papers.what_was_done: Counterfactual distributions under multiple time point interventions are defined by the g-computation formula obtained from a factorized likelihood, and causal effects are read off as features of regimen-specific means, including nonparametric marginal structural models for static rules and for rules that respond to time-dependent covariates. Estimation proceeds by super learning an initial fit of each g-computation factor, then applying a parameter-specific fluctuation submodel to each factor and iterating the maximum likelihood update to convergence, which makes the estimator consistent if either the initial fit or the fluctuation function is consistent. The framework states directly why an untargeted super learner fails: cross-validation is optimal for the global loss-specific dissimilarity while the variance of the target parameter is of smaller order than the variance of the nuisance fit. The proposed remedy is a targeted loss, specifically the square of the efficient influence curve evaluated at the true treatment mechanism, used as the cross-validation criterion for selecting among targeted estimators; that criterion is available where the treatment mechanism is known, as in a sequentially randomized trial. Inference uses the empirical covariance of the efficient influence curve as a working normal model. A targeted dimension reduction of the covariate history is proposed and its bias and variance cost is flagged. No data, no sample size and no simulation appear in this part.

future_research.gap: Time-dependent covariate and outcome processes are collected in nearly all trials and are not used in the causal analysis; implementation is deferred.
future_research.quote: Even though almost all current clinical trials collect time dependent data, these important sources of information have been ignored in the assessment of the causal effect of a drug or

problems.evidence: The mismatch is named exactly: cross-validation optimizes a global loss-specific dissimilarity while the variance of the causal parameter is of smaller order than the variance of the nuisance fit, so an optimally cross-validated fit of the longitudinal factors yields an overly biased substitution estimator. A concrete replacement is supplied, the square of the efficient influence curve as a targeted loss whose cross-validated risk equals the asymptotic variance of the resulting estimator. It does not close the entry: that loss is evaluated at the true treatment mechanism, so the criterion is exact only where the mechanism is known, and Part I contains no simulation or data showing how much a prediction-optimal fit loses against a targeted one.
problems.quote: This is due to the fact that cross-validation makes optimal choices w.r.t. the (global) loss-function specific dissimilarity, but the variance of Ψ(Qn ) is of smaller order than the variance of Qn itself.

problems.evidence: The framework is presented as an exceptionally powerful basis for assessing causal effects, but every guarantee it carries is conditional on the causal graph assumptions and the sequential randomization that define the g-computation formula in the first place. Double robustness protects against misspecification of the nuisance fits, not against a covariate history that fails to block the confounding paths, and the exposition does not separate the two.
problems.quote: provides an exceptional powerful framework for assessing causal effects, with distinct advantages relative to other proposed methodology

problems.evidence: Selection among targeted estimators is itself an open choice indexed by the initial fit, and the answer offered is another layer of cross-validation. Nothing establishes that a targeted maximum likelihood estimator is the default a longitudinal emulation should use, and no comparison is reported against the weighted and g-computation estimators it is set against.
problems.quote: Selection among different targeted maximum likelihood estimators (e.g., indexed by different initial estimators) can be based on loss-based crossvalidation

problems.evidence: Inference rests on asymptotic linearity with influence curve evaluated at the true treatment mechanism, and the variance is the empirical covariance of that curve at the fitted nuisance and the true mechanism. In an emulation where the mechanism is estimated rather than known, and where the data structure has been expanded across many time points, that plug-in is not the correct variance, and no scalable alternative is given.
problems.quote: the T-MLE is consistent and asymptotically linear with influence curve

papers.title: Evaluating dose response from flexible dose clinical trials.
papers.one_line: Weighting two flexible-dose olanzapine trials with 234 and 172 patients reversed an apparent negative dose response, while exposing that some dose sequences the estimand contemplates could never occur under the protocol and that a few weights above 100 drove the answer.
papers.what_was_done: Two randomized double-blind flexible-dose trials, 234 patients with bipolar mania on olanzapine 5 to 20 mg per day and 172 with schizophrenia on 10 to 20 mg per day, were reanalyzed to recover a dose response that the unweighted comparison by last or modal dose reported as negative. Time-dependent weights were the product of a stabilized inverse probability of the observed dose sequence and a stabilized inverse probability of remaining on treatment, and the weighted repeated-measures model showed no strong dose effect and in places reversed the apparent negative one. Among pretreatment covariates only baseline severity predicted dose assignment; among post-baseline variables, change in outcome and, weakly, adverse events did. Adverse events would have been dropped by a prediction-targeted model selection with cross-validation and were kept deliberately. In the bipolar trial a few weights above 100 dominated the estimates and were removed or truncated at limits of 10, 20 and 50 with similar results; in the schizophrenia trial all weights fell between 0 and 5. Dose was grouped in three intervals at 10, 15 and 20 mg and then in two, with coarser intervals chosen to avoid zero probabilities and finer ones to control selection better. The experimental treatment assignment condition was judged partly violated because the protocol permits only single-step titration, so an abrupt 5 to 20 mg profile is unattainable.

future_research.gap: The estimand that matters for practice is a dynamic titration regimen, but eliciting the titration rule from a protocol that states none and estimating its effect in trials of this size is unsolved.
future_research.quote: It may be more relevant from a public health perspective to evaluate potential outcomes associated with certain flexible dynamic regimens

problems.evidence: Rather than stopping at the weight distribution, the analysis names the unsupported history: an abrupt jump from 5 to 20 mg cannot occur because the protocol allows one increment per step, so the estimated probability of that dose sequence is zero and the corresponding regimen is not in the data. That is the identification of a specific unsupported patient history the entry asks for. It does not close the entry: the naming is ad hoc rather than the output of a procedure, the weights above 100 in the bipolar trial are still handled by truncation without saying whose histories they were, and no threshold separates a tolerable violation from a fatal one.
problems.quote: In our analysis, the ETA assumption may have been partially violated in that some dose profiles (e.g. abruptly changing dose from 5 to 20 mg) would not be attainable in a flexible dose trial

problems.evidence: The equivalence classes of dose were set by a tradeoff between positivity and confounding control rather than by clinical meaning: three intervals at 10, 15 and 20 mg, then two at 10 to 15 and 20, with the coarser grouping chosen because it avoids zero probabilities. A dose response estimated over classes selected on that criterion answers a question defined by the estimation problem, not by the pharmacology.
problems.quote: larger intervals would avoid the trouble of having zero probability associated with certain potential dose configuration, finer intervals may achieve better control over selection bias

problems.evidence: Flexible dosing is a dynamic regime in practice, since physicians titrate on response and tolerability, but the protocol records no rule beyond permitting reduction for adverse events at the physician's discretion. With 234 and 172 patients, recovering the implicit rule and estimating its effect is stated to be out of reach, so the analysis falls back to static fixed-dose contrasts that nobody administered.
problems.quote: in absence of clearly defined rules in the protocol, it appears that elicitation of such rules and estimating associated potential outcomes from flexible dose trials of relatively small size may pose difficulties

problems.evidence: Adverse events were a weak predictor of dose and a cross-validated selection targeting prediction error would have removed them, yet they were kept because overfitting the dose model is the safer error for confounding control. The two objectives point in opposite directions on the same variable, and the resolution here was judgment rather than a criterion tied to bias in the dose effect.
problems.quote: AEs were a rather weak predictor that would have been eliminated had we used aggressive search algorithms with cross-validation or other model selection tools that target prediction error

problems.evidence: The intended target is what patients would experience under a fixed dose, but no fixed-dose assignment exists in these trials; what the weighting delivers is a contrast among dose sequences that occurred with nonzero estimated probability, after some sequences were declared unattainable. The result is a data-defined estimand acknowledged as questionable from a public health standpoint even while being treated as the regulatory gold standard.
problems.quote: our strategy was to use IPTW MSM methodology to mimic potential outcomes that one would expect had patients been randomized to fixed dose groups

papers.title: Causal inference in longitudinal studies with history-restricted marginal structural models.
papers.one_line: History-restricted marginal structural models replace the full exposure history with a user-chosen window of length s, and the choice of s is stated to remain subjective while determining both the estimand and the statistical power.
papers.what_was_done: A class of marginal structural models is formalized in which the causal contrast is indexed by exposure over a fixed window of s periods immediately preceding outcome collection rather than over the whole follow-up, and inverse-probability-weighted, g-computation and doubly robust estimators are shown consistent under the same four assumptions used for ordinary marginal structural models: existence of counterfactuals, consistency, time ordering and sequential randomization. The motivating application evaluates whether California Air Resources Board regulations since 1980 produced measurable health benefits in the Los Angeles Basin, with quarterly ambient ozone, nitrogen oxides and particulate matter over 84 quarters across 195 grids of 10 by 10 kilometers, and quarterly hospital discharges and mortality as outcomes. A g-computation fit plots the effect of one year of ozone exposure on asthma discharges in children aged 0 to 19 as a function of season and calendar time; part of the winter curve has the wrong sign, attributed to uncontrolled confounding, measurement error or misspecification, and no confidence intervals are reported. Choosing s is governed by subject-matter judgment, computational tractability and power, with larger s reducing power and tractability. A survival variant is shown to break: treatment-specific survival curves cannot be recovered from history-restricted hazards.

future_research.gap: In practice the chosen window will usually be shorter than the true carryover period, so the maximum lag effect stays unknown.
future_research.quote: The second case scenario is most likely to occur in practice, since statistical power and implementation considerations often will prevent investigation of the causal effects of treatment histories that are too long.

problems.evidence: The window length s is the single parameter that defines which exposure history the causal contrast refers to, and its selection is stated to remain subjective after all the offered guidance is applied. The illustrated fit uses one year of ozone exposure over quarterly data, a choice made from prior belief about lag rather than from any outcome-blind procedure, and no rule prevents s from being revised once the estimates are seen.
problems.quote: Nevertheless, choosing a suitable value for s based on these guidelines remain subjective and may lead to two scenarios

problems.evidence: When s is shorter than the true carryover period, which is stated to be the usual case, the estimand silently becomes the effect of the last s periods rather than the effect of exposure, and the maximum lag remains unknown. The reported quantity is therefore defined by an analyst-chosen window and by what the data can support, not by the scientific question, yet it is reported as the effect of one year of ozone.
problems.quote: even if the causal effect of the treatment over time will not be completely described

problems.evidence: For failure-time outcomes the history-restricted hazard cannot be mapped back to a treatment-specific survival curve, because hazards at different times correspond to different restricted regimens and the conditioning covariate set changes with time. A hazard contrast reported under this model therefore compares different sets of survivors and has no risk-scale counterpart, which is exactly the substitution the entry describes.
problems.quote: In this variant of HRMSMs, treatment-specific survival curves cannot be computed

problems.evidence: Power is stated to fall as the window lengthens because a longer history defines a more complex contrast that fewer observed sequences support, so the study of a scientifically adequate lag is traded against having enough information to estimate anything. With 84 quarters across 195 grids the nominal data volume is large, yet the window that the analysis can actually support is set by the informative sequences that survive weighting.
problems.quote: the statistical power to investigate the causal effect of interest will likely decrease when considering larger history sizes s

problems.evidence: The intervention is a body of air quality regulation, the exposure is a quarterly ambient pollutant concentration, and the unit carrying that exposure is a 10 by 10 kilometer grid rather than a person, while outcomes are population discharge and mortality rates for the same grid-quarter. Neither the versions of the regulation nor the mapping from an areal exposure to an individual assignment is defined, and demographic in-migration is folded into calendar time as a proxy confounder.
problems.quote: The geographic area of interest was divided into 195 10 x 10 km grids, based on know patterns of air pollutants and meteorology in the LA Basin.

papers.title: Causal analysis of case-control data.
papers.one_line: Three weighting schemes applied to the same oral contraceptive and myocardial infarction case-control data give odds ratios of 2.82, 2.83 and 3.34, with no criterion offered to choose among them.
papers.what_was_done: Indirect standardization of case-control data is recast as an inverse-probability-weighted estimator so that the standardized morbidity ratio taking the exposed as standard becomes a weighted odds ratio with an explicit target population, the exposed. The construction assumes a stationary source population over the recruitment period, taken to be acceptable when recruitment lasts no more than two or three years, and requires that the stratifying variable is not affected by exposure and that no confounding remains within its strata. Empirical weights assign each exposed subject a weight of one and each unexposed subject the exposure odds among controls in the stratum; regression weights replace the stratum odds with the fitted odds from a logistic model of exposure fitted on the controls only, avoiding the small and zero cells that full cross-classification produces. On an incidence case-control study of oral contraceptives and myocardial infarction, standard logistic regression gave an odds ratio of 2.82 (95% CI 1.70 to 4.68) and Mantel-Haenszel gave 2.82 (1.70 to 4.69); the regression-weighted generalized estimating equations fit gave 3.34 (2.15 to 5.21) while the empirically weighted fit gave 2.83 (1.82 to 4.41). No sensitivity analysis addresses stationarity, misclassification or the residual confounding all four estimates assume away.

future_research.gap: Stationarity of the source population is assumed implicitly in case-control practice and is not checked.
future_research.quote: the stationary population assumption appears to be made routinely

problems.evidence: On one dataset, empirical weights give 2.83 (1.82 to 4.41) and regression weights give 3.34 (2.15 to 5.21), an 18 percent difference in the point estimate produced solely by how the same weight was computed. Both are described as valid implementations of the same estimator and no argument, diagnostic or criterion is offered for preferring one, nor is any requirement stated that a study report both.
problems.quote: Interestingly, when empirical weights were used instead of regression weights, the odds ratio estimate (which equals s OR ) was 2.83 (95% CI: 1.82,4.41).

problems.evidence: Fitness of the data for the causal reading rests on the source population being stationary in size and incidence, and the threshold offered is a narrative one: recruitment of no more than two or three years is likely to be approximately satisfactory. There is no test on the data, no quantity to compute and no value that would stop the analysis, only a rule of thumb about duration.
problems.quote: Provided that T is not too large, say no more than two or three years, this assumption is likely to be approximately satisfied in practice.

problems.evidence: Cross-classifying multiple confounders is abandoned because it produces cells with small or zero entries, and the fix is to smooth over those cells with a logistic model of exposure fitted on the controls. The unsupported strata are thereby replaced by extrapolated fitted odds without being enumerated, which is exactly the substitution of a modeling device for a statement about which histories the data support; the 3.34 estimate is the one this smoothing produces.
problems.quote: this may lead to cells with small or zero entries, resulting in instability of estimates

problems.evidence: The example asserts in a single clause that two variables suffice for confounding control and that no misclassification or other bias operates, then reports intervals conditional on all three holding. Stationarity, sufficiency of the adjustment set and absence of misclassification differ sharply in whether any evidence could bear on them, and all three enter the report identically.
problems.quote: we assume that age (AGE) and cigarettes (CIG) are sufficient to control confounding and that there is no misclassification or other source of bias

problems.evidence: Variance after weighting depends on a software convention: whether the weights must be rescaled so that their sum across cases matches the number of cases varies by generalized estimating equation implementation, and getting it wrong changes the reported interval rather than the point estimate. That is a correctness detail carried in the software rather than in a stated estimator.
problems.quote: it may be necessary to scale the weights such that their sum across all cases equals the actual number of cases

problems.evidence: One component of the target-versus-estimate gap is closed explicitly: the weighted summary is shown to correspond to the exposed as standard population, so it retains a causal reading even under effect modification, whereas the Mantel-Haenszel weights are shown to correspond to no recognizable population at all. It does not close the entry: the remaining components, loss from mapping the source population onto a stationary idealization and estimation error, are not separated from that one, and the reported interval mixes them.
problems.quote: With s OR the target population is clearly specified (namely, the exposed population)
